summary: An IAB statement that, even though RFC 1597 reserves address space for private networks, any enterprise that expects to connect to the Internet should apply for globally unique addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: If two houses in different towns use the same address, the mail gets lost when they meet. Get your own address if you plan to meet.

subtitle: Why enterprises should apply for globally unique IP addresses.

tldr.problem: RFC 1597 reserved address space for private networks that would never connect to the Internet. Some enterprises thought they could use private addresses and avoid the registration process, but this creates problems when (or if) they later need external connectivity.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and IANA issue guidance to Internet registries: even though private addresses exist, any enterprise that anticipates external connectivity should apply for globally unique addresses if they meet the allocation criteria.
tldr.outcome: The IAB clarifies that globally unique addresses are necessary for Internet connectivity, and enterprises should plan accordingly. Registries are encouraged to allocate unique addresses without unreasonable conditions to enterprises that expect future connectivity.

today: RFC 1814 is Informational guidance from the IAB and remains relevant. Many organizations did end up using private addresses without planning for eventual connectivity, and some faced expensive renumbering projects. The recommendation to apply for unique addresses early proved prescient. Today, with IPv6 providing ample address space, the pressure for private address reuse has diminished, but the core principle remains sound: enterprises should plan their addressing strategy from the start.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
RFC 1597 established reserved IP address space for private networks that are isolated and will never connect to the Internet. These private addresses can be reused within many different organizations without conflict, since they never appear in Internet routing.

However, some enterprises saw this as a way to avoid registering for global addresses. Elise Gerich, on behalf of the IAB and IANA, clarifies the guidance: any enterprise that anticipates external connectivity should apply for globally unique addresses instead.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 1597 said: use secret addresses if you are never connecting. But some companies used them anyway, thinking they could switch later. This RFC says: get real addresses from the start if you might connect.

sections.title: Guidance to Registries
sections.content:
The IAB advises Internet registries to allocate globally unique addresses according to the established criteria in RFC 1466, without letting the existence of private address space discourage it. Registries should verify that an organization meets the size requirements and submits a reasonable engineering plan, then make the allocation.

Organizations should be informed of the provisions in RFC 1597 so they understand the trade-off. Large enterprises requiring external connectivity should apply for large blocks of unique addresses. Smaller enterprises with a few hosts needing external connectivity can receive addresses from their Internet service provider or, if necessary, directly from the registry.

The key point: globally unique addresses are necessary to differentiate between destinations on the Internet. A unique address by itself does not guarantee global connectivity—service providers may place restrictions on what they route—but it is a prerequisite.
sections.plainLanguage: Registries should give out real addresses generously to any company that might want to connect. You cannot meet the Internet later with a fake address.

sections.title: Planning for Future Connectivity
sections.content:
Enterprises that use private addresses and later decide to connect to the Internet may face renumbering: converting all their addresses to globally unique ones across all their machines. This is expensive and disruptive.

The RFC recommends that any organization anticipating external connectivity apply for globally unique addresses early. The registry will ask for a realistic deployment schedule and evidence of attention to address conservation, but these criteria are reasonable and should not be obstacles.

Even if an enterprise is unsure whether it will connect, the prudent path is to obtain unique addresses and use them from the start. This avoids the pain of renumbering later.
sections.plainLanguage: It is cheaper to get real addresses now than to swap them out later on every computer when you do connect.
